**In Praise of Noticing: A Field Guide to Ordinary Wonder**

I want to write about mornings.

Not the grand, Instagram-filtered kind of morning with perfect light pouring over a mountain cabin and a cup of coffee held just-so in both hands. I mean the real ones. The Tuesday ones. The ones where your alarm goes off a little too early and the room is a little too cold and your socks don't match and you stand in the kitchen half-asleep waiting for the kettle to boil, listening to it click and hum like it's clearing its throat to start the day.

There's a whole universe in that moment if you let there be.

I used to rush through it. I think most of us do. We treat mornings like a hallway we have to get through to get to the "real" part of the day - work, school, errands, news, noise. We scroll while brushing our teeth. We half-listen to podcasts at 1.5x speed while making toast. We are efficient. We are optimized. We are exhausted.

A few years ago, I started practicing something very small and very unfashionable: paying attention on purpose, with no productivity goal attached. Not mindfulness as an app with streaks and badges. Just noticing. Looking out the window a little longer. Listening to the rain without also doing something else. It sounds trivial. It changed everything.

Because attention is love, in its quietest form. Whatever you pay attention to, you are saying: you matter enough for me to pause for you.

Let me tell you what I've noticed.

I've noticed that light has moods. Morning light in September is different from morning light in March. September light is golden and low and a little nostalgic, like it's remembering summer. It slants through blinds in stripes and makes dust motes look like tiny planets drifting. March light is paler, more tentative, like it's asking permission. Seven a.m. light in winter is blue and thin and honest. It doesn't flatter, but it tells the truth.

I've noticed that every neighborhood has a soundscape if you stand still long enough to hear it. Where I live, it's dogs first, then cars, then kids, then a leaf blower that someone fires up with great confidence at 8:12 every Saturday. There's a crow that lives on my street who has exactly three opinions and shares all of them loudly before 7 a.m. There's an old man who walks past humming, always the same tune I can't quite place, like a song from a commercial in 1978. I never introduced myself, but I feel like we have a relationship. He hums, I listen from behind my curtains with my coffee. We're good.

I've noticed that people are kinder in small, invisible ways than the news would have you believe. The barista who remembers that you like oat milk even though you only come in twice a month. The stranger who holds the elevator even though it would have been easier to pretend they didn't see you running. The teenager who gave up his seat on a crowded bus without making a big show of it, just stood up, nodded, looked out the window. That kind of kindness doesn't trend. It doesn't get filmed. But it's load-bearing. It's what holds the whole rickety structure of public life together.

If you want a free education in humanity, ride public transit and watch. Not stare - watch gently. People are novels walking around in sneakers. That woman with the giant tote bag full of library books? She's probably going home to a quiet apartment with a cat and strong opinions about translators. That guy in the construction vest asleep with his head against the window, mouth slightly open? He got up at 4:30 to build something you will walk through and never think about. That kid with headphones on, mouthing lyrics, tapping his fingers on his backpack? He's in the middle of the best three minutes of his day. We are all extras in each other's movies and protagonists in our own, and every once in a while, on a good day, you remember that.

Libraries taught me this best. I love libraries the way some people love churches. It's not just the books, though the books are a miracle stacked on a miracle. It's the permission. A library says: you can just be here. You don't have to buy anything. You don't have to be productive or pretty or successful. You can sit in a comfortable chair and read about black holes or baking or the history of Venice and no one will ask you what it's for. My favorite sport is wandering the stacks with no plan, pulling out a book because the spine is an interesting shade of green, opening to a random page. I have learned more from accidental pages than from any curriculum.

Once I found a note in a library book. It was in a collection of Mary Oliver poems, on the page with "The Summer Day," the one that ends, "Tell me, what is it you plan to do / with your one wild and precious life?" Someone had underlined it in pencil and written in the margin, in shaky handwriting: "Call Mom." I sat there for a long time. I still think about that stranger. I hope they called.

Notes like that are everywhere if you look. Grocery lists left in carts: eggs, spinach, birthday candles, dog treats. That tells a whole story, doesn't it? Someone is trying to be healthy, someone is having a birthday, someone is loved with fur. Doodles on napkins. A shoe left on the side of the highway with no explanation. A child's lost mitten pinned to a fence by a kind neighbor so it can be found. The world is constantly leaving little messages for itself, little breadcrumbs of care.

I think we underestimate how much we need beauty that is useless. Not beauty that improves your brand or your home value, but beauty that just sits there being beautiful for no reason. The way frost makes ferns on a windshield. The way a parking lot puddle can hold the entire sunset if you crouch down. The way fresh snow squeaks under boots, that high, clean sound like Styrofoam singing. The smell of a bookstore. The smell of rain on hot pavement - petrichor, scientists call it, from the Greek for "stone" and "the blood of the gods." Even dirt smells divine when it rains.

And food. Can we talk about toast for a second? Really good toast - thick bread, real butter melting into all the little holes, a pinch of flaky salt - is a completely reasonable reason to be happy to be alive. A ripe peach in August that drips down your chin. The first bite of something your grandmother made, tasting exactly like childhood. We eat so often on autopilot, standing over the sink, scrolling. What if we sat down? What if we actually tasted? Pleasure is not frivolous. It's information. It's your body saying: stay, this is good, there is good here.

I'm not trying to be naive. I know the world is heavy right now. I read the headlines too. The climate, the wars, the rent, the loneliness, the feeling that everything is fraying at the edges. Noticing small beauty doesn't fix any of that. It doesn't lower the temperature of the planet or stop injustice. But I don't think it's escapism, either. I think it's fuel.

You cannot protect what you do not love, and you cannot love what you do not notice. The people who fight hardest for a neighborhood, for a park, for a river, for a neighbor, are the people who have paid attention to it. They know the names of the trees. They know which stoop gets the evening sun. Attention turns space into place, and place into home, and home into something worth showing up for.

So here's my modest proposal for a better life, with no morning routine to buy and no 5 a.m. club to join: once a day, notice one thing on purpose.

Notice the exact color of the sky at 6 p.m. Is it periwinkle? Ash? Peach sherbet? Notice how your friend's eyes crinkle when they really laugh, not the polite laugh. Notice the weight of your dog's head on your foot. Notice the way your own hands look - the veins, the scars, the story of everything they've carried. Notice the cashier's name. Use it. Notice when you feel most like yourself, and try to do more of that, even if it's only for ten minutes.

Write it down if you want. I keep a ridiculous little notebook I call "Small Goods." Every night I write three tiny good things. Not gratitude-list performative things like "family, health, home," though those are true. I mean specific, weird, sensory things. Tuesday: the bus driver waited for me. The pear was perfect. My sock stayed up all day. Wednesday: heard a kid tell his dad a joke about a potato and both of them lost it. Found a dollar in an old coat. The moon looked photoshopped. It's silly. It works. On bad days, I flip back through and remember that even the worst weeks were studded with small lights.

I'll end with a moment I still carry.

Last autumn I was on a train, tired, late, crammed in with everyone else staring at phones, the air stuffy with wet coats and quiet irritation. The train stopped in the middle of nowhere between stations - signal problems, the conductor mumbled. Everyone sighed collectively. We sat. A minute passed. Then, out the left side of the train, the sun began to set over a field. Not a famous field. Just a flat, ordinary field with a couple of bare trees. But the light hit it and the whole thing turned gold, then pink, then a deep, burning orange that reflected in all the windows. Without anyone saying anything, people started looking up from their phones. A little girl stood up on her seat and gasped. An old man across from me smiled and said, almost to himself, "Well, would you look at that." And for maybe ninety seconds, a whole car full of strangers just watched the sky together in silence.

Then the train lurched forward. Phones came back out. Life resumed. But something had softened. People made eye contact. Someone laughed. It was nothing. It was everything.

That's what I want to write about, freely, given a thousand words and no assignment: that. The ninety seconds when we all look up at the same light and remember we're in this together, on this strange, spinning, beautiful rock, hurtling through darkness, sharing snacks and sunsets and seats.

Keep looking up.
